title: The Nazareth manifesto (Luke 4:14–21)
hook: he unrolls Isaiah: good news to the poor, sight to the blind, freedom for the oppressed
tomorrow: to the edge of the cliff

segments.voice: Yesterday, the desert, and the devil leaving until an opportune time. Your line was until another time. Did your weakest hour show up, and were you ready? Day five hundred sixteen.

A small-town synagogue on the sabbath. Everyone knows everyone. And today the young man who was brought up here, Joseph's son, is back home, and word about him has spread through the region. Luke says he went into the synagogue on the sabbath day, "as his custom was." He stands up to read. The attendant hands him a scroll, the prophet Isaiah. And here's a detail Luke slows down for: he unrolls it, looking for a particular place. He's choosing his words. Luke has said he was already teaching in synagogues, but this is the first time Luke lets us hear what he says.

He reads, in the King James words: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised, To preach the acceptable year of the Lord." Count who's in it. The poor. The brokenhearted. The captives. The blind. The bruised, the crushed and oppressed. Five kinds of people, and not one of them powerful. That's why some readers call this the Nazareth manifesto: a mission statement, read out at the start. Some readers hear in the acceptable year of the Lord an echo of the jubilee in Leviticus, the fiftieth year, when liberty was proclaimed and land went back to its families. Then Luke slows everything down: "And he closed the book, and he gave it again to the minister, and sat down. And the eyes of all them that were in the synagogue were fastened on him." Everyone waits. And then one sentence: "This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears." This day. Not someday, for those five kinds of people: now, in the room where they're sitting. And there's a quiet detail you can check for yourself. Set Luke beside Isaiah 61, and you'll see he stops reading mid-verse, just before Isaiah's next words, the day of vengeance of our God. Christians read that pause in different ways, but it's there.
screen: `THE SPIRIT OF THE LORD IS UPON ME.`
`HE SAT DOWN; EVERY EYE ON HIM.`
then, large: `THIS DAY IS THIS SCRIPTURE FULFILLED IN YOUR EARS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick one of the five to act on. Settle, and breathe. Let the list come back slowly, one at a time, and wait a breath with each. The poor: someone short of money. The brokenhearted: someone grieving or lonely. The captive: someone stuck, in debt, in prison, in a habit. The blind: someone who can't see a way forward. The bruised: someone pushed down by others. Notice if one of these has a face. Let it be someone you actually know, or someone you pass every week. Then choose one small thing you can do for them today, not someday. If you pray, you can hold that person before God. If you don't, simply hold them in mind. The bell holds the time.
Jubilee. The Levitical year of liberty and land returned, echoed in the acceptable year of the Lord that Jesus read about himself.
Your line: today this is fulfilled. Do your one small thing for your one person before the sun goes down, and let it be today's, not someday's. Day five hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Some Christian groups working with the poor, prisoners and the sick point to Luke 4:18–19 as their charter, and in the Revised Common Lectionary the passage is read in the season after Epiphany.

fork.setup: you're reading Isaiah 61 aloud in your hometown synagogue. the next words are about a day of vengeance. what do you do?
options: read on to the end of the chapter.
stop, close the book, sit down, and say it's fulfilled today.
fork.reveal: he stops just before the day of vengeance, closes the book, sits down, and says: this day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears.

original.note: Greek: release, letting go. in Luke 4:18 it stands behind both deliverance and liberty.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice reading from the Bible at church.
what it means: the first teaching Luke lets us hear names the poor, the captive, the blind and the crushed as the heart of his work, starting today.
what a scholar hears: "set at liberty them that are bruised" comes from Isaiah 58, woven into Isaiah 61, and the reading stops just before the day of vengeance.

sources.quoted: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised, To preach the acceptable year of the Lord.
And he closed the book, and he gave it again to the minister, and sat down. And the eyes of all them that were in the synagogue were fastened on him.
This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears.

notes: 'To heal the brokenhearted' is in the KJV's Greek text but absent from many manuscripts. The 'five kinds of people' count follows the KJV.
The jubilee link for 'acceptable year' is a common scholarly reading, framed as 'likely'.
'The scroll was handed by the attendant' paraphrases 'minister' (hyperetes). Confirm.
Stopping before 'the day of vengeance of our God' (Isaiah 61:2) is widely noted; interpretations vary.
'Manifesto' is the index title's word, used descriptively.

Editor review (2026-10-01): SERIOUS repetition and accuracy fixes. Day 500 already taught this same scene (Luke 4:16–21) with the same 4:20/4:21 quotes, the semeron 'today' angle (shepherds to the cross), the same fork and the same σήμερον original; this day now drops semeron and centers the five kinds of people and the stop before the day of vengeance, with a new fork, match pair, myth and original (ἄφεσις). Also: 'the carpenter's son' replaced by Luke's 'Joseph's son' (4:22); 'his first public statement in Luke' corrected (4:15 says he was already teaching in synagogues); the jubilee described per Leviticus 25 (liberty, land returned), not 'debts released' (that is the sabbatical year, Deuteronomy 15); cut 'sitting was the teacher's posture', 'scholars notice', invented benches, and the 'habit of showing up' echo of day 511.
